label: to/from (honorific “에게”)
meaning_en: The honorific counterpart of “에게/한테”: it marks a person to be respected as the receiver of an action (“to”), and, with verbs of receiving, as its source (“from”): “할아버지께 드리다, 부모님께 받다”.
usage: It attaches to a noun for a person who deserves respect (“선생님께, 부모님께, 사장님께, 할머니께”). The matching verbs are the honorific ones: “드리다” (give), “여쭙다/여쭈다” (ask), “말씀드리다” (tell), “전해 드리다”; with the plain “주다”, the sentence sounds off. The subject marker for the honoured person is “께서” (a different row). With verbs of receiving it names the source: “부모님께 용돈을 받다”.

examples.en: I wrote a letter to my mother.
I asked the teacher a question.
I gave my grandfather a birthday present.
I received an allowance from my parents.
Please pass this document on to the boss.

compare.difference: “에게” is the neutral particle for people; “께” is its honorific replacement for someone you respect.

pair.en: I gave my younger sibling a present.
I gave my grandmother a present.

compare.difference: “께서” marks the honoured person as the subject of an action; “께” marks that person as the one the action goes to.

pair.en: The teacher came.
I went to the teacher.

pitfalls.note: With “께”, the honorific verb “드리다” is used, not “주다”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my grandfather a present.

pitfalls.note: “께” is only for a person to be honoured; for a friend or younger person use “에게”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my younger sibling a present.

topik_tip: The honorific set goes together: “께”, “드리다”, “께서”, “-시-”.

label: every, each
meaning_en: A particle meaning “every, each”: it says that something holds for each member of a set, without exception. It is used for times (“주말마다”), people (“사람마다”) and places (“집집마다”), and for intervals (“십 분마다”).
usage: It attaches to a noun without a space. Time nouns give “every ...” (“날마다, 아침마다, 주말마다”), people and things give “each one differs / has” (“사람마다 생각이 다르다”), a duration gives the interval (“십 분마다 한 대씩”). The nouns can be doubled (“집집마다”). After a verb the structure is “-ㄹ 때마다” (each time ...), not “마다” alone.

examples.en: I go to the library every weekend.
Each person thinks differently.
I take a walk in the park every morning.
Every shop in front of the school was full of customers.

examples.ko: 버스는 십 분마다 한 대씩 온다.
examples.en: A bus comes every ten minutes.

compare.difference: “주말에” says “on the weekend” (one time frame); “주말마다” says “every weekend”, each one of them.

pair.en: I go to the library on the weekend.
I go to the library every weekend.

compare.difference: “매일” and “날마다” are near-synonyms. “마다” combines with any noun, while “매” is limited to time words (“매일, 매주, 매번”).

pair.en: I exercise every day.
I exercise every day.

pitfalls.note: It attaches to a noun, without a space.
pitfalls.en: I go to the library every weekend.

pitfalls.note: After a verb, “마다” does not work alone: use “-ㄹ 때마다”.
pitfalls.en: Every time we meet, we say hello.

topik_tip: “N마다” (each N) and “-ㄹ 때마다” (every time) are the two frames that exams use.

label: only (with a negative)
meaning_en: A particle meaning “nothing but, only N”, and it always works with a negative predicate: “N밖에 없다, N밖에 못 하다, N밖에 안 -다”. The sentence stresses that N is all there is, and often that this is too little.
usage: It attaches to a noun or a counter phrase: “천 원밖에 없다”, “한 명밖에 안 왔다”, “영어밖에 못 한다”. The predicate has to be negative or say “없다/모르다/못 -다/안 -다”. For a positive sentence “만” is used. It often tells that the amount is small, which adds a feeling (“십 분밖에 안 남았다”). The phrase “하나밖에 없는” (the only one there is) is a frequent collocation.

examples.en: I have only 1,000 won in my wallet.

examples.ko: 시험 시간이 십 분밖에 안 남았다.
examples.en: Only ten minutes are left in the exam.

examples.ko: 이 일을 할 수 있는 사람은 지수밖에 없다.
examples.en: Jisu is the only one who can do this work.
I can speak only English.
This is a present that exists only once in the world.

compare.difference: “만” is also “only” but works with a positive predicate. “밖에 + negative” usually carries the feeling that it is too little.

pair.en: Only one person came.
Only one person came.

compare.difference: “밖에 없다” and “뿐이다” are near-synonyms. “뿐” closes the sentence with “이다”, “밖에” needs a negative.

pair.en: There is no one I can trust but you.
You are the only one I can trust.

pitfalls.note: The predicate must be negative.
pitfalls.en: I have only 1,000 won.

pitfalls.note: With a verb of action, add “안/못”.
pitfalls.en: Only one person came.

topik_tip: “밖에” always needs a negative; if the predicate is positive, the particle is “만”.

label: like (manner, resemblance)
meaning_en: A particle that attaches to a noun and means “like N, as N does”: it compares the manner, look or level of something to N. In “마치 N처럼” it makes the comparison explicit (“as if”).
usage: It attaches to a noun with no space: “새처럼 날다, 아이처럼 웃다, 눈처럼 하얗다, 가수처럼 노래하다”. After a verb the shape is “-는 것처럼” (“아는 것처럼 말하다”). The set phrase “마치 ...처럼” strengthens it. “같이” is a near-synonym (see the level-3 lesson); “만큼” compares degree, not manner. It is also used with “너처럼, 나처럼” for comparisons with people.

examples.en: Jisu sings as well as a singer.

examples.ko: 눈처럼 하얀 구름이 하늘에 떠 있다.
examples.en: Clouds as white as snow float in the sky.
I want to be a warm person like my mother.
I smiled broadly like a child.
Time passed by just like a dream.

compare.difference: In similes “처럼” and “같이” are near-synonyms and swap freely; the time-noun phrases (“매일같이”) are only “같이”.

pair.en: The hands are as cold as ice.
The hands are as cold as ice.

compare.difference: “처럼” compares manner or look; “만큼” compares degree.

pair.en: I want to sing like you.
I want to sing as well as you.

pitfalls.note: After a verb, use “-는 것처럼”, not “처럼” alone.
pitfalls.en: They spoke as if they knew.

pitfalls.note: It attaches directly to the noun.
pitfalls.en: I want to fly like a bird.

topik_tip: Do not confuse it with “만큼”: “처럼” is about how, “만큼” about how much.

label: starting from (place, point)
meaning_en: A particle that marks a starting point and stresses it: “from N (onward), starting from N”. It is the emphatic form of “에서”, often paired with “까지” for a range, or used in “여기서부터” (from here on).
usage: It attaches to a place or a point of origin: “집에서부터 학교까지”, “서울에서부터 부산까지”, “처음부터”. After “여기, 거기, 어디” the contracted form “서부터” is normal in speech (“여기서부터는, 어디서부터”). It marks only the beginning of a stretch or a process: unlike “에서”, it cannot mean “at (a place)”. It cannot mark a person as the source: use “에게서/한테서”.

examples.ko: 집에서부터 학교까지 걸어서 삼십 분 걸린다.
examples.en: It takes thirty minutes on foot from home to school.
From here on, we have to go on foot.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 어디서부터 시작해야 할지 모르겠다.
examples.en: I do not know where to begin with this problem.
I traveled by bicycle all the way from Seoul to Busan.
The story began from childhood.

compare.difference: “에서” also marks the place where an action happens; “에서부터” only marks where something starts.

pair.en: I walked here starting from home.
I studied at home.

compare.difference: “부터” marks a starting point in time or order (“아침부터”); “에서부터” adds place and origin.

pair.en: It rained from the morning.
It rained starting from Seoul.

pitfalls.note: It does not mark a person as the source; use “에게서”.
pitfalls.en: I received a present from a friend.

topik_tip: “여기서부터, 거기서부터, 어디서부터” are the contracted forms to know.

label: onto, into (placing); on top of that
meaning_en: A particle for the place where something is put: “on, onto, into N”. It goes with verbs of placing, and it can also mean “in addition to N”.
usage: It attaches to a place noun, with a placing verb: “놓다, 넣다, 두다, 붙이다, 쓰다, 적다, 담다, 버리다”. It is the colloquial, slightly stronger form of “에”, shortened to “에다”. In “N에다가 M까지/도” it means “on top of N, also M”. For a destination of motion (“가다, 오다”) the plain “에” is used.

examples.en: I put the book on the desk.
Please write this name here.
Trash has to be thrown into the trash can.
I ate rice and kimchi on top of that, so I am full.
I put the food in the refrigerator.

compare.difference: With a placing verb the two are near-synonyms. “에다가” is colloquial and works only with such verbs, while “에” also covers time and motion.

pair.en: I put the book on the desk.
I put the book on the desk.

compare.difference: “에다가” goes with the place something is put; “에서” goes with the place an action takes place.

pair.en: I put the book in the bag.
I took the book out of the bag.

pitfalls.note: It does not go with a verb of motion toward a place.
pitfalls.en: I went to school.

topik_tip: “에다가” with placing verbs is the spoken way to say “on / into”.

label: toward (a person)
meaning_en: A particle meaning “toward, to (a person)”, with a sense of direction: movement, attention or feeling heading toward someone. It is “에게” plus the directional “로”.
usage: It attaches to a person or animal: “엄마에게로, 지수에게로”. The verbs show direction: “달려가다, 다가가다, 돌아가다, 향하다, 쏠리다, 오다”. It is somewhat written and expressive. For giving, telling and sending, “에게” alone is used. The spoken variant is “한테로”. For a place destination, use “(으)로” or “에”.

examples.en: The child ran to the mother.
Everyone's attention turned to Jisu.
Their gaze turned toward me.
The puppy approached its owner.

examples.ko: 지영이는 오랜 방황 끝에 가족에게로 돌아왔다.
examples.en: After long wandering, Jiyoung returned to the family.

compare.difference: “에게” marks the recipient; “에게로” adds the direction of movement toward the person.

pair.en: I sent a letter to my friend.
I ran toward my friend.

compare.difference: “한테로” is the spoken counterpart; the meaning is the same.

pair.en: I ran to Mom.
I ran to Mom.

pitfalls.note: For giving or telling, use “에게”, not “에게로”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my friend a present.

pitfalls.note: For a place, use “(으)로”.
pitfalls.en: I went to Seoul.

topik_tip: “에게로” follows verbs of movement or attention; “에게” follows verbs of giving.

label: from (a person)
meaning_en: A particle that marks a person as the source from which something comes: “from N”. It goes with receiving, hearing, learning and borrowing verbs, and with “오다” for something that arrives from a person.
usage: It attaches to a person or animal: “친구에게서, 부모님에게서”. Typical verbs: “받다, 듣다, 배우다, 빌리다, 얻다, 오다, 나오다”. It is the written or neutral form; the spoken form is “한테서”. For honorific sources the particle is “께”, for places “에서”, for formal writing “으로부터”. Note that “에게” alone with “받다” can also mark a giver, but with “오다” only “에게서” marks the sender.

examples.en: I received a birthday present from a friend.
I heard old tales from my grandmother.
I learned this technique from a senior.
I borrowed 10,000 won from my younger sibling.
Children learn a lot from their parents.

compare.difference: With “오다” the two differ: “에게서” marks who the letter comes from, “에게” who it comes to.

pair.en: A letter came from my friend.
A letter came to my friend.

compare.difference: “에게서” is the written and neutral one, “한테서” the spoken one. The meaning is the same.

pair.en: I heard from my friend.
I heard from my friend.

pitfalls.note: The giver takes “에게서”; the one who is given something takes “에게”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my friend a present.

pitfalls.note: A place or an institution takes “에서”, not “에게서”.
pitfalls.en: I borrowed a book from the library.

topik_tip: Check the direction: from a person is “에게서”, to a person is “에게”.

label: from (a person), spoken
meaning_en: The spoken form of “에게서”: it marks a person as the source of something received, heard, learned or borrowed: “친구한테서 전화가 왔다”.
usage: It attaches to a person or animal: “친구한테서, 엄마한테서, 선배한테서”. Typical verbs: “받다, 듣다, 배우다, 빌리다, 얻다, 오다”. Often shortened in speech to “한테” (“친구한테 들었어”). It is colloquial: in writing and speeches “에게서” or “으로부터” is chosen. For places or institutions the particle is “에서”.

examples.en: I got a call from a friend yesterday.
I heard this story from Mom.
I returned the book I had borrowed from my younger sibling.
I got useful information from a senior.
Who did you hear that news from?

compare.difference: The meaning is the same; “에게서” fits writing, “한테서” fits speech.

pair.en: I received a present from a friend.
I received a present from a friend.

compare.difference: “한테서” marks the source; “한테” marks the receiver.

pair.en: A call came from my friend.
A call came to my friend.

pitfalls.note: A place or an institution takes “에서”.
pitfalls.en: I borrowed money from the bank.

pitfalls.note: The giver takes “한테서”; the receiver takes “한테”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my friend a book.

topik_tip: In speech, “한테서” is often shortened to “한테”: the verb (“받다”, “듣다”) tells you the direction.

label: or; as many as; or something
meaning_en: A particle with three related jobs: “N이나 M” (N or M, a choice), a number or amount followed by “이나” (as many as, surprisingly much), and “N이나” for a so-so option (“let's just ... or something”).
usage: After a consonant it is “이나”, after a vowel “나”. Choice: “커피나 차”. Amount: “한 시간이나 기다렸다” (waited a full hour). So-so option: “영화나 볼까?” (shall we watch a movie or something?). The three readings differ by context: two nouns give a choice, a counter gives surprise at the large amount, a single noun with a suggestion gives a casual option. The lexical partner for emphasis on a small amount is “만”.

examples.en: Let's talk over coffee or tea.
I waited for the bus for a whole hour.
I'm bored; shall we watch a movie or something?
On the weekend I plan to read a book or something at home.

examples.ko: 그 가게에서 옷을 열 벌이나 샀다.
examples.en: I bought as many as ten pieces of clothing at that shop.

compare.difference: “영화나 볼까?” offers a casual choice; “영화라도 볼까?” suggests the film as a minimum, at least something.

pair.en: Shall we drink coffee or something?
Shall we at least have some coffee?

compare.difference: After an amount, “이나” stresses that it is a lot; “만” limits it.

pair.en: I waited a whole hour.
I waited only an hour.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “나”.
pitfalls.en: Please give me coffee or tea.

pitfalls.note: After a consonant the particle is “이나”.
pitfalls.en: Shall we read a book or something?

topik_tip: Read the context: two nouns mean “or”, a counter means “as many as”, a lone noun in a suggestion means “or something”.

label: or (alternatives)
meaning_en: A connective ending that gives alternatives: “do X or Y”. Either of the two may happen, and the main verb applies to whichever is chosen. Repeated, “-거나 -거나” means “whether ... or ...”.
usage: It attaches to any verb, adjective or “이다” stem with no vowel change and takes “-었-” if needed (“학생이거나”, “갔거나”). The two halves are alternatives, not a sequence: for “do X and then Y” use “-고”. A typical frame is “-거나 -거나 하다” (do things like X or Y), and “-거나 말거나” means “whether or not” (“가거나 말거나”). The noun counterpart is “N(이)나 N”.

examples.ko: 주말에는 보통 책을 읽거나 영화를 봐요.
examples.en: On weekends I usually read a book or watch a movie.
If you feel sleepy or tired, take a short break.

examples.ko: 비가 오거나 눈이 오거나 학교에 가야 한다.
examples.en: Rain or snow, I have to go to school.

examples.ko: 모르는 것이 있으면 선생님께 물어보거나 인터넷에서 찾아보세요.
examples.en: If there is something you do not know, ask the teacher or look it up online.
Whether Minjun comes or not, it makes no difference to me.

compare.difference: “-거나” and “-든지” are near-synonyms for “or”. “-든지” leans on the freedom to choose either.

pair.en: I drink coffee or tea.
Have coffee or tea, whichever you like.

compare.difference: “N(이)나 N” joins two nouns; “-거나” joins two verb phrases.

pair.en: I drink coffee or tea.
I drink coffee or I drink tea.

pitfalls.note: It gives alternatives, not a sequence; for “and then” use “-고”.
pitfalls.en: I ate and went to school.

topik_tip: Look for two choices joined by “-거나”; the frame “-거나 -거나 하다” means doing things like these.

label: background, contrast (“and”, “but”)
meaning_en: A connective ending with a soft link: it sets the background for the next clause (“I did X, and ...”), gives a mild contrast (“X, but ...”), or leads into a question or request (“I am hungry; shall we ...?”).
usage: Verbs and “있다/없다” take “-는데”, adjectives and “이다” take “-ㄴ/은데” (“예쁘다 → 예쁜데”, “멀다 → 먼데”, “춥다 → 추운데”, “학생이다 → 학생인데”), and the past stem takes “-었는데”. A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “ㄴ”: “살다 → 사는데”, “길다 → 긴데”. The second clause may be a statement, a question or a request. It is less strict than “-지만” (“but”), and it can end the sentence as “-는데(요)”.

examples.ko: 어제 서울에 갔는데 비가 많이 왔어요.
examples.en: I went to Seoul yesterday, and it rained a lot.
I am hungry; would you like to have lunch together?
This outfit is pretty, but it is too expensive.

examples.ko: 집이 먼데 걸어서 갈 수 있을까요?
examples.en: My house is far; can I go on foot?

examples.ko: 내일 시간 있는데 같이 영화 볼래요?
examples.en: I am free tomorrow; do you want to watch a movie together?

compare.difference: “-지만” is a firm “but”. “-는데” may only set the scene and can lead to a question or request.

pair.en: This outfit is pretty, but expensive.
This outfit is pretty, but expensive.

compare.difference: In the middle of a sentence it is “-는데1”. At the end of a sentence it is the exclamation or hanging ending “-는데2”.

pair.en: It is raining; do you have an umbrella?
It is raining, though.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은데”, not “-는데”.
pitfalls.en: This outfit is pretty, but expensive.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem adjective drops the ㄹ: “멀다” becomes “먼데”.
pitfalls.wrong: 집이 멀은데 걸어서 갈 수 있을까요?
pitfalls.right: 집이 먼데 걸어서 갈 수 있을까요?
pitfalls.en: My house is far; can I go on foot?

topik_tip: “-는데” links without committing to “but” or “so”: the context supplies the relation.

label: if, when
meaning_en: A connective ending for a condition or a recurring time: “if X, Y” and “whenever/when X, Y”. It covers possible conditions, habits and general truths.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-면”, after other consonants “-으면”. Real stems: “오다 → 오면”, “먹다 → 먹으면”, “살다 → 살면” (the ㄹ stays, no “으”), “눕다 → 누우면” (ㅂ-irregular), “듣다 → 들으면” (ㄷ-irregular), “학생이다 → 학생이면”; past “-었으면” for an imagined or completed condition. The second clause may be a statement, an invitation or a command. A frequent frame is “-으면 되다” (it is enough to ...).

examples.en: If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
When spring comes, flowers bloom.
If you have time, do you want to watch a movie together?
If there is anything you do not know, ask at any time.
You just press this button.

compare.difference: With a command or a proposal as the main clause “-거든” and “-으면” are near-synonyms; “-으면” also handles facts and habits.

pair.en: Call me when you arrive.
Call me once you arrive.

compare.difference: “-으면” sets a condition or the first time something happens; “-을 때” points to the time during which something is going on.

pair.en: I will call once I get home.
I will call when I am going home.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular verb turns ㅂ into “우”.
pitfalls.en: If I lie down on the bed, I fall asleep at once.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem takes “-면” without “으”.
pitfalls.en: It is convenient if you live in Seoul.

topik_tip: Choose the form by the final sound: vowel or ㄹ gives “-면”, other consonants give “-으면”.

label: while doing; at the same time
meaning_en: A connective ending for two actions or states at the same time: “while doing X, Y”, “X and also Y”. With “도” it makes a contrast: “-으면서도” (even though).
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-면서”, after other consonants “-으면서”; it takes verbs and adjectives. The subject of both clauses is the same, and the first verb has no tense ending. Real stems: “걷다 → 걸으면서”, “듣다 → 들으면서”, “살다 → 살면서”, “가볍다 → 가벼우면서”, “알다 → 알면서도”. For different subjects the pattern is “-는 동안”. A written variant is “-(으)며”.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
Talking on the phone while walking is dangerous.
Jisu answered with a smile.
This laptop is light and also performs well.
I pretended not to know, even though I knew.

compare.difference: “-고” simply strings actions in order. “-으면서” says they happen together.

pair.en: We talked while eating.
We ate and then talked.

compare.difference: “-으며” is a near-synonym that is more written; both mean “while”.

pair.en: They spoke with a smile.
They spoke with a smile.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular verb turns ㄷ into ㄹ before “-으”.
pitfalls.en: I study while listening to music.

pitfalls.note: Both clauses share the subject; for different subjects use “-는 동안”.
pitfalls.en: While I cooked, my younger sibling cleaned.

topik_tip: Same subject, two simultaneous actions: that is “-으면서”.

label: so that, in a way that (purpose)
meaning_en: A connective ending giving the purpose, manner or result of the main verb: “so that X, in a way that X”. The subject of the “-게” clause can differ from the subject of the main clause.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems with no vowel change: “깨지 않다 → 깨지 않게”, “크다 → 크게”, “보이다 → 보이게”. The ㄹ stays: “길다 → 길게”. It turns an adjective into an adverb (“예쁘게 웃다”). Set phrases: “맛있게 드세요” (enjoy your meal), “재미있게 보내세요”.

examples.ko: 아이가 깨지 않게 조용히 문을 닫았다.
examples.en: I closed the door quietly so as not to wake the child.
I wrote the letters big so that they could be seen well.
Dress warmly so that you do not catch a cold.
Please enjoy it before it gets cold.
I kept it secret so that my friends would not be startled.

compare.difference: In the purpose use “-게” and “-도록” are near-synonyms; “-도록” is more formal and also means “until”.

pair.en: I wrote it big so that it could be seen well.
I wrote it big so that it could be seen well.

compare.difference: “-게” allows a different subject in the two clauses. “-으려고” needs the same subject.

pair.ko: 아이가 잘 수 있게 불을 껐다.
pair.en: I turned off the light so that the child could sleep.
I turned off the light to go to sleep.

pitfalls.note: The purpose clause states the wished result: “catch a cold” does not fit a good purpose.
pitfalls.en: Dress warmly so that you do not catch a cold.

topik_tip: The same “-게” turns adjectives into adverbs (“크게, 예쁘게”) and introduces a purpose clause.

label: stop and switch to another action
meaning_en: A connective ending for an action or state that is interrupted and replaced by another: “X-ing, then (stopped and) Y”. With a past form it means “did X, then went back/reversed: X-었다가 Y”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems: “먹다 → 먹다가”, “걷다 → 걷다가” (the ㄷ stays), “놀다 → 놀다가”. The subject is the same in both clauses. A past stem (“-었다가”) says that the first action was completed and then undone or followed by a reverse action (“갔다가 돌아오다”, “켰다가 끄다”). A short form “-다” also exists. The related “-다가1(2)” of the level-3 list covers events that break in during an activity.

examples.en: I was eating, and went out to take a call.
If you get tired while studying, take a short break.
I went to Seoul and came back this morning.
I turned on the air conditioner, but it was cold, so I turned it off again.
On my way home I stopped by the supermarket.

compare.difference: “먹다가” says the eating was interrupted; “먹고” says it was finished before the next action.

pair.en: I left in the middle of eating.
I ate and then left.

compare.difference: The plain “-다가” interrupts an action in progress; “-었다가” turns back after the action is done.

pair.en: I rested on the way to Seoul.
I went to Seoul and came back.

pitfalls.note: “-었다가” does not mean an interruption; for “was doing, then stopped”, use the plain stem.
pitfalls.en: I was eating and went out to take a call.

topik_tip: Compare “가다가” (on the way) and “갔다가” (went and came back): the past stem changes the meaning.

label: turning a verb into a noun
meaning_en: An ending that makes a verb or adjective into a noun for an activity: “읽다 → 읽기” (reading), “말하다 → 말하기”. It also forms frames such as “-기 쉽다/어렵다/좋다” and “-기 바라다”.
usage: It attaches to any stem without a vowel change; the ㄹ stays (“만들다 → 만들기”, “살다 → 살기”). The resulting noun takes particles (“달리기를 좋아하다”, “읽기가 어렵다”). Fixed frames: “-기 쉽다” (easy to), “-기 어렵다”, “-기 좋다”, “-기 싫다”, “-기 시작하다”, “-기 바랍니다” (a formal request), “-기 전에”. The names of the TOPIK sections are made this way too: “듣기, 읽기, 쓰기, 말하기”.

examples.en: I like running in the morning.
In Korean, speaking is harder than reading.

examples.ko: 이 책은 글씨가 커서 읽기 쉽다.
examples.en: This book has large print, so it is easy to read.
Yeongsu has started writing a diary these days.
Please submit the report by tomorrow.

compare.difference: “-기” and “-는 것” both turn a verb into a noun phrase. “-기” is shorter and fixed in frames like “-기 쉽다”; “-는 것” is the freer form.

pair.en: I like running.
I like running.

pitfalls.note: The verb does not stand alone as an object: it needs “-기”.
pitfalls.en: I like running.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-기”.
pitfalls.en: This dish is hard to make.

topik_tip: The section names of TOPIK (“듣기, 읽기, 쓰기, 말하기”) are good examples of this “-기”.

label: present modifier (the one who does)
meaning_en: An adnominal ending that makes a verb a modifier of a noun in the present: “the person who eats”, “the school I attend”. It is also used with “있다/없다” (“맛있는, 없는”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems and to “있다/없다” and their compounds: “먹다 → 먹는”, “가다 → 가는”, “맛있다 → 맛있는”, “모르다 → 모르는”. A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ: “살다 → 사는”, “알다 → 아는”, “만들다 → 만드는”. Adjectives take “-ㄴ/은” instead (“예쁜 꽃”). It describes an action that is going on or habitual, so “읽는 책” is “the book being read, or the book one reads”.

examples.en: This is the school I attend.
I want to eat delicious Korean food.

examples.ko: 저기서 책을 읽는 사람이 제 동생이에요.
examples.en: The person reading a book over there is my younger sibling.
I went to meet a friend who lives in Seoul.
Ask next time about what you do not know.

compare.difference: “-는” is the present modifier, “-은/-ㄴ” the past one.

pair.en: The person who is eating is Minjun.
The person who ate is Minjun.

compare.difference: “-을/-ㄹ” is the prospective modifier.

pair.en: It is the book I read.
It is the book I will read.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-는”.
pitfalls.en: I met a friend who lives in Seoul.

pitfalls.note: An adjective does not take “-는”.
pitfalls.en: I bought pretty flowers.

topik_tip: The three modifiers: present “-는”, past “-은/-ㄴ”, future “-을/-ㄹ”.

label: past modifier (the one that did)
meaning_en: An adnominal ending that makes a verb a modifier of a noun for a completed action: “the movie I saw”, “the person I met”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: after a vowel it is “-ㄴ” (“보다 → 본”, “가다 → 간”), after a consonant “-은” (“먹다 → 먹은”). A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “ㄴ” (“만들다 → 만든”, “알다 → 안”, “살다 → 산”; note that “산” can also come from “사다”). It is the modifier of “-ㄴ 후에, -ㄴ 적이 있다, -ㄴ 다음에”. An action in progress or repeated in the past takes “-던”.

examples.en: The book I read yesterday was really fun.

examples.ko: 친구에게서 받은 선물을 책상 위에 놓았다.
examples.en: I put the present I got from my friend on the desk.

examples.ko: 이 책은 제가 도서관에서 빌린 책이에요.
examples.en: This book is the one I borrowed from the library.
Who was the person you met yesterday?

examples.ko: 다 먹은 그릇은 여기에 놓아 주세요.
examples.en: Please put the empty bowls here.

compare.difference: “-은” points to a finished action, “-을” to one that is still to come.

pair.en: The food I ate yesterday was tasty.

pair.ko: 내일 먹을 음식은 아직 안 샀다.
pair.en: I have not yet bought the food I will eat tomorrow.

compare.difference: “-은” is a finished event; “-던” is an action that was ongoing, repeated or left unfinished.

pair.en: I returned the book I read.
I returned the book I was reading.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-ㄴ”.
pitfalls.en: I ate the cake that Jisu made.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the ending is “-ㄴ” written in the syllable.
pitfalls.en: The movie I saw yesterday was fun.

topik_tip: A past modifier of a verb is “-ㄴ/은”; the same ending on an adjective is the present.

label: prospective modifier (the one to do)
meaning_en: An adnominal ending that makes a verb modify a noun for an action not yet done, planned or possible: “the book to read today”, “the place to go”, “time to rest”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ”, after other consonants “-을”: “읽다 → 읽을”, “가다 → 갈”, “살다 → 살” (the ㄹ and “-ㄹ” merge), “만들다 → 만들”. It modifies nouns like “계획, 생각, 때, 수, 것, 시간, 곳, 일”: “할 일, 쉴 시간, 갈 곳”. The same shape is the base of “-을 것이다, -을 수 있다, -을 때”. Adjectives take it for a possible or supposed state (“좋을 때”).

examples.en: I put the book to read today into my bag.

examples.ko: 내일 만날 사람은 어릴 때 친구예요.
examples.en: The person I am meeting tomorrow is a friend from childhood.

examples.ko: 저녁에 먹을 음식을 사러 마트에 갔다.
examples.en: I went to the supermarket to buy food for dinner.
I am looking for a house to live in from now on.

examples.ko: 할 일이 너무 많아서 쉴 시간이 없어요.
examples.en: I have so much to do that I have no time to rest.

compare.difference: “-는” is the present modifier, “-을” the one for what is yet to happen.

pair.en: It is the book I read.
It is the book I will read.

compare.difference: “-은” is for finished actions.

pair.en: The person I met yesterday is Jisu.
The person I will meet tomorrow is Jisu.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem merges the ㄹ with “-ㄹ”.
pitfalls.en: I am looking for a house to live in from now on.

pitfalls.note: A prospective modifier does not take a past form.
pitfalls.wrong: 내일 만난 사람은 어릴 때 친구예요.
pitfalls.right: 내일 만날 사람은 어릴 때 친구예요.
pitfalls.en: The person I am meeting tomorrow is a friend from childhood.

topik_tip: “할 일, 갈 곳, 쉴 시간”: frequent nouns after this modifier are worth learning as units.

label: modifier of adjectives (present)
meaning_en: An adnominal ending that makes an adjective (or “이다”) a modifier of a noun: “small bag”, “high mountain”, “good person”. For adjectives it describes the present state; for verbs the same shape is a past modifier.
usage: After a vowel it is “-ㄴ”, after a consonant “-은”. Real stems: “작다 → 작은”, “높다 → 높은”, “좋다 → 좋은”, “크다 → 큰”, “춥다 → 추운” (ㅂ-irregular), “길다 → 긴” and “멀다 → 먼” (the ㄹ drops), “학생이다 → 학생인”. Adjectives “있다/없다” compounds (“맛있다, 재미없다”) take “-는” instead (“맛있는, 재미없는”). Adjectives have no separate past modifier in the plain form: a past state is “-었던”.

examples.en: I put my wallet in a small bag.
If you climb a high mountain, the view is good.
On cold days I drink warm tea.
I cut my long hair short.
I want to move to a bigger room.

compare.difference: Verbs take “-는” for the present (“읽는 책”); adjectives take “-ㄴ/은” (“좋은 책”).

pair.en: It is the book I read.
It is a book I like.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ/은” describes what a thing is like now; “-던” recalls what it used to be like.

pair.en: A pretty child is smiling.
The child who used to be pretty has grown up.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우”.
pitfalls.en: On cold days I drink warm tea.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem adjective drops the ㄹ before “-ㄴ”.
pitfalls.en: I cut my long hair short.

topik_tip: The list has this “-은” separately from the past “-은2”; the stem type (adjective or verb) tells which one it is.

label: turning a word into a noun (state, result)
meaning_en: An ending that makes a verb or adjective into a noun for a state, result or feeling (“기쁨, 믿음, 웃음”), and in notices, minutes and headlines ends a clause in note style (“내일은 휴관임”).
usage: After a vowel it is “-ㅁ” written on the syllable (“기쁘다 → 기쁨”, “아프다 → 아픔”), after a consonant “-음” (“웃다 → 웃음”, “믿다 → 믿음”). A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ and adds “ㅁ”: “살다 → 삶”, “알다 → 앎”, “만들다 → 만듦”. A ㅂ-irregular stem becomes “움”: “어렵다 → 어려움”. “이다” gives “임”. Many words are fixed nouns (“꿈, 걸음, 죽음, 삶”); for ordinary activities “-기” is used. The note-style ending is for written notices.

examples.ko: 친구에 대한 믿음은 하루아침에 생기지 않는다.
examples.en: Trust in a friend does not form overnight.
The sound of the child's laughter echoed down the corridor.

examples.ko: 한 걸음 한 걸음 천천히 올라갔다.
examples.en: I climbed slowly, step by step.
Tomorrow is a regular closing day.
Life is a succession of choices.

compare.difference: “-기” names an activity (“달리기”), “-음” a state or result (“기쁨”). Many verbs have only one of the two as a noun.

pair.en: Running is good for health.
Laughter is good for health.

compare.difference: “-는 것” is the free way to make a noun clause; “-음” gives a single noun or a note-style ending.

pair.en: Laughing is good for health.
Laughter is good for health.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps the ㄹ and adds “ㅁ”.
pitfalls.en: Life is a succession of choices.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective becomes “움”.
pitfalls.en: I went through many difficulties.

topik_tip: In notices and exam passages, the final “-음/-ㅁ” on a clause (“휴관임”, “금지함”) is the written note style.

label: noting a new fact (“I see”)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that voices a newly noticed or newly learned fact: “I see, so ...”, “oh, ... is the case”. The polite form is “-는군요”.
usage: Verbs and “있다/없다” take “-는군” (“오다 → 오는군”), adjectives and “이다” take “-군” (“맛있다 → 맛있군”, “어렵다 → 어렵군”, “학생이다 → 학생이군”), the past takes “-었군” (“왔군”). A ㄹ-stem verb drops the ㄹ before “-는” (“살다 → 사는군”). With a polite listener it is “-군요”. It expresses the speaker's own discovery, so it is not used for facts one has known for a long time. “그렇군요” is the set reply “I see”.

examples.en: Oh, it is already snowing.
This restaurant's food is really delicious, I see.
The roads are especially jammed today, I see.
The work is harder than I thought.
Oh, I see. I did not know.

compare.difference: “-는군” and “-는구나” both voice a discovery and are near-synonyms. “-는군” has the polite form “-는군요”; “-는구나” is the “해라체” form.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing.
Oh, it is snowing.

compare.difference: The two are near-synonyms, and each has a polite form (“-네요”, “-는군요”); “-네” is the more frequent in speech.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing.
Oh, it is snowing.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-군”, not “-는군”.
pitfalls.en: It is cold, I see.

pitfalls.note: A past stem takes “-군”, not “-는군”.
pitfalls.en: It rained yesterday, I see.

topik_tip: Use the polite “-군요” to anyone you address politely: the bare “-군” sounds like talking down or to oneself.

label: I will (promise to the listener)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with which the speaker promises or announces to the listener what they will do: “I will ...”. The decision is made with the listener in mind, as an offer or commitment.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ게”, after other consonants “-을게”; it attaches to verb stems, and the polite form is “-을게요”. Real stems: “가다 → 갈게”, “먹다 → 먹을게”, “놀다 → 놀게”, “만들다 → 만들게”, “듣다 → 들을게”. The subject is the speaker. It is not used with adjectives or in questions (“-을까?” asks). The reply “알았어, 그렇게 할게” is a typical collocation.

examples.en: I will go first. Call me later.
This time I will buy the coffee.
I will contact you as soon as I arrive.
From next time I will come early.
Okay. I will do that.

compare.difference: “-을게” is a promise to the listener. “-을래” voices what the speaker wants to do, and can ask about the listener's wish.

pair.en: I will go first.
I want to go first.

compare.difference: “-겠-” (“제가 하겠습니다”) is a formal declaration of will; “-을게요” is the everyday promise.

pair.en: I will do it.
I will do it.

pitfalls.note: The subject is the speaker: it cannot be a third person.
pitfalls.en: I will go.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem merges the ㄹ with “-ㄹ”.
pitfalls.en: I will hang out with a friend today.

topik_tip: It is a promise addressed to someone: for a bare decision, the pattern is “-겠-”.

label: confirming, “right?”, “you know”
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that checks something the speaker thinks the listener knows or shares: “..., right?”, “..., isn't it?”. It also states what is obvious (“물론이지”) and, with “그래”, gives a gentle suggestion (“-지 그래?”). The polite form is “-지요/-죠”.
usage: It attaches to any stem, including “이다” and past stems (“좋지?”, “학생이지”, “갔지?”). The ㄹ of an ㄹ-stem stays (“알다 → 알지”, “살다 → 살지”). Rising intonation asks for confirmation; falling intonation states something that is clear. “-지 그래?” (“Why don't you ...?”) is a mild advice. For listeners you speak politely to, use “-지요/-죠”. “-죠” is the contraction used in speech.

examples.en: The weather is really nice today, isn't it?
Studying Korean is hard, but it is fun, you know.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 어제 회사에 안 왔지?
examples.en: That person did not come to the office yesterday, right?
Of course. I will help you.
If you are hungry, why don't you eat first?

compare.difference: “-지” checks with the listener or states what is clear; “-네” notes something new.

pair.en: The food here is good, isn't it?
The food here is good.

compare.difference: “-지” is a neutral check. “-잖아” says that the listener already knows it, often with a hint of reproach.

pair.en: You know that, right?
You know that, remember?

pitfalls.note: With someone you speak politely to, use “-지요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, the weather is nice today, isn't it?

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-지”: the ㄹ drops only before certain endings such as “-ㄴ” or “-ㅂ”.
pitfalls.en: You know this song too, right?

topik_tip: The list's four labels (statement, question, command, request) are all “-지” in different intonation.

label: soft exclamation, hanging remark
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that offers a remark with a soft touch of admiration, surprise or objection and leaves room for the listener to respond: “...(, you know)”, “that suits you, doesn't it?”. It also asks a question with the same softness (“뭘 먹었는데?”). The polite form is “-는데요”.
usage: Verbs and “있다/없다” take “-는데”, adjectives and “이다” take “-ㄴ/은데”, the past takes “-었는데”: “오다 → 오는데”, “어울리다 → 어울리는데”, “좋다 → 좋은데”, “멀다 → 먼데”, “학생이다 → 학생인데”. It is the “해체” form: with a person you speak politely to, add “요”. The same form between clauses is the connective “-는데1”; at the end of a sentence it hangs.

examples.ko: 그 옷이 너한테 정말 잘 어울리는데.
examples.en: That outfit really suits you.

examples.ko: 이 사람 피아노를 정말 잘 치는데?
examples.en: This person really plays the piano well.
Wow, it is snowing a lot.
If we go now, we will be late, you know.
I am fine with that too, though.

compare.difference: “-네” notes something plainly; “-는데” leaves the sentence hanging for the listener's reaction.

pair.en: It is snowing a lot, isn't it.
It is snowing a lot.

compare.difference: A flat statement ends with “-다”; “-는데” softens it and invites a response.

pair.en: I am hungry, you know.
I am hungry.

pitfalls.note: With someone you speak politely to, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, the weather is really nice today.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은데”, not “-는데”.
pitfalls.en: That bag is really pretty.

topik_tip: At the end of a sentence “-는데” never means “but” alone: it gives a hint that something follows or a reaction is expected.

label: noting something (“oh, ...”)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that voices something the speaker has just noticed or realised, or a mild evaluation: “oh, it is ...!”, “...! (I see)”. The polite form is “-네요”.
usage: It attaches to any stem, including “이다” and the past: “오다 → 오네”, “예쁘다 → 예쁘네”, “학생이다 → 학생이네”, “갔다 → 갔네”. A ㄹ-stem verb drops the ㄹ before “ㄴ” (“살다 → 사네”). It is common in speech with “-네요” to polite listeners, and typical for compliments (“잘하시네요”). It is for new information the speaker has just taken in, not for what they have long known.

examples.en: It is already twelve o'clock.
The food here is good.
Oh? It is raining.
You speak Korean really well.
Wow, the view here is really good.

compare.difference: “-는군” and “-네” both note a discovery. “-네” is the lighter and more frequent in speech.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing.
Oh, it is snowing.

compare.difference: “-네” notes something new; “-지” checks something the listener should share.

pair.en: The food here is good.
The food here is good, right?

pitfalls.note: It voices a new discovery, so it does not fit a fact about oneself that one has always known.
pitfalls.en: I am Korean.

pitfalls.note: With someone you speak politely to, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, you speak Korean well.

topik_tip: “-네요” is the polite noting form; many compliments in conversation use it.

label: I'd like to; do you want to?
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that states what the speaker wants or has decided to do (“I think I'll ...”), or asks about the listener's wish (“do you want to ...?”). It is spoken and personal. The polite form is “-을래요”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ래”, after other consonants “-을래”; it attaches to verb stems. Real stems: “마시다 → 마실래”, “먹다 → 먹을래”, “놀다 → 놀래” (the ㄹ stays), “만들다 → 만들래”, “듣다 → 들을래”. In statements the subject is the speaker (“나는 커피 마실래”); in questions it is the listener. The negative “안 -ㄹ래” refuses (“안 갈래”). It does not fit formal speeches.

examples.ko: 나는 커피 마실래. 너는 뭐 마실래?
examples.en: I will have coffee. What will you have?
I think I will rest at home today.
Would you like to watch a movie together?

examples.ko: 나는 안 갈래. 너 혼자 가.
examples.en: I am not going. You go alone.
What do you want to eat for lunch?

compare.difference: “-을래” voices what the speaker wants. “-을게” promises something to the listener.

pair.en: I want to go first.
I will go first.

compare.difference: “-을래?” asks what the listener wants. “-을까?” proposes something for both.

pair.en: Do you want to go together?
Shall we go together?

pitfalls.note: With someone you speak politely to, add “요”: “드실래요?”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, would you like some coffee?

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ: “놀다” becomes “놀래”.
pitfalls.en: I will hang out with my friends today.

topik_tip: “-을래?” is a question about the listener's will; “-을까?” is a proposal for both.

label: come to be; end up
meaning_en: An expression for a change that comes about through circumstances rather than one's own plan: “come to X, end up X-ing, it turns out that ...”. It is also used for polite announcements (“결혼하게 되었습니다”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems with “게 되다”, where “되다” carries the tense (“-게 되었다/됐다, -게 된다”): “가다 → 가게 되다”, “알다 → 알게 되다”, “좋아하다 → 좋아하게 되다”. It describes an outcome that was not chosen, or one that is presented that way for politeness. The expression is written with a space. For a plan that was decided, “-기로 하다” is used. For a change in an adjective's state the pattern is “-어지다”.

examples.en: I have ended up moving to Seoul this year.

examples.ko: 한국 드라마를 보다가 한국어를 좋아하게 됐다.
examples.en: From watching Korean dramas, I came to like Korean.
We are getting married next month.

examples.ko: 이 일을 하면서 많은 사람을 알게 되었다.
examples.en: Doing this work, I came to know many people.

examples.ko: 비가 와서 소풍을 못 가게 됐어요.
examples.en: Because of the rain, we ended up not being able to go on the picnic.

compare.difference: “-기로 하다” is a decision someone made. “-게 되다” is how things turned out.

pair.en: I decided to go to Korea.
I ended up going to Korea.

compare.difference: “-어지다” is a change of an adjective's state; “-게 되다” is a development with a verb.

pair.en: Korean has become easier.
I came to live in Korea.

pitfalls.note: It is written with a space: “-게 되다”.
pitfalls.en: I came to know that person.

topik_tip: A fixed way to report news politely: “-게 되었습니다” (it has come to be that ...).

label: because (formal, written)
meaning_en: An expression for a reason: “because X, Y”. It states a cause plainly and is common in writing and in formal speech. With a noun it is “N 때문에”, and at the end of a sentence “-기 때문이다” (it is because ...).
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems, after a tense ending if needed: “오다 → 오기 때문에”, “갔다 → 갔기 때문에”, “성실하다 → 성실하기 때문에”, “공휴일이다 → 공휴일이기 때문에”. The main clause is a statement, not a command or suggestion (“-으니까” is used then). A noun cause is “N 때문에” (“교통사고 때문에”). The closing form “그 이유는 -기 때문이다” gives the reason after the fact.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 오기 때문에 경기가 취소되었다.
examples.en: The match was canceled because it rained a lot.

examples.ko: 지수는 성실하기 때문에 모두에게 신뢰를 받는다.
examples.en: Jisu is trusted by everyone because Jisu is diligent.

examples.ko: 어제 늦게 잤기 때문에 오늘 너무 피곤하다.
examples.en: I went to bed late yesterday, so I am very tired today.

examples.ko: 내일 시험이 있기 때문에 오늘은 도서관에서 공부해야 한다.
examples.en: I have an exam tomorrow, so today I have to study at the library.

examples.ko: 제가 늦은 이유는 길이 막혔기 때문입니다.
examples.en: The reason I was late is that the road was jammed.

compare.difference: “-어서” is the everyday reason ending. “-기 때문에” is more formal and stresses the reason.

pair.en: I was tired, so I went to bed early.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.

compare.difference: “-으니까” can be followed by a command or a suggestion; “-기 때문에” cannot.

pair.en: It is raining, so take an umbrella.
The match was canceled because it rained.

pitfalls.note: A command or suggestion does not follow “-기 때문에”; use “-으니까”.
pitfalls.en: It is raining, so take an umbrella.

pitfalls.note: After a noun, “이다” is needed: “N이기 때문에”.
pitfalls.en: Because today is a public holiday, they are closed.

topik_tip: Reason frames in TOPIK: “-기 때문에” (formal, written) versus “-어서” (everyday) versus “-으니까” (allows commands).

label: decide to, agree to
meaning_en: An expression for a decision or an agreement about a future action: “decide to X, resolve to X, agree to X”. It is used both for one's own resolution and for what two or more people have settled on.
usage: It attaches to verb stems and is followed by a verb of deciding, mostly “하다” in the past (“-기로 했다”); “-기로 약속했다/결심했다/마음먹었다” are variations. The plan can be about oneself (“운동하기로 했다”) or a joint arrangement (“내일 만나기로 했다”). A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ (“만들다 → 만들기로”). The negative is “-지 않기로 하다”.

examples.en: I decided to exercise every day from this year.

examples.ko: 우리는 내일 아침 아홉 시에 만나기로 하고 헤어졌다.
examples.en: We agreed to meet at nine tomorrow morning and parted.

examples.ko: 친구와 같이 제주도로 여행을 가기로 약속했다.
examples.en: I promised my friend that we would go on a trip to Jeju Island together.
I resolved not to be late from now on.

examples.ko: 이번 주말에는 가족과 함께 시간을 보내기로 하였다.
examples.en: I decided to spend this weekend with my family.

compare.difference: “-기로 하다” is a decision someone made; “-게 되다” is how things came out.

pair.en: I decided to go to Korea.
I ended up going to Korea.

compare.difference: “-으려고 하다” is an intention that is in progress or about to happen; “-기로 하다” is a settled decision or agreement.

pair.en: I plan to get up early tomorrow.
I have decided to get up early tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: A modifier does not go before “로”: the stem takes “-기” directly.
pitfalls.en: I decided to go tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-기”.
pitfalls.en: I decided to make the food.

topik_tip: Choose “-기로 하다” for a decision or agreement, and “-게 되다” for an outcome that was not chosen.

label: it seems; I think
meaning_en: An expression for a guess or a softened opinion: “it seems that, it looks like, I think”. It is based on what the speaker sees, hears or feels, and it also makes an opinion or a feeling less direct (“이게 더 좋은 것 같아요”).
usage: The modifier shows the time: present verb “-는 것 같다” (“오는”), past verb “-ㄴ/은 것 같다” (“온”), future or supposition “-ㄹ/을 것 같다” (“올”), adjective “-ㄴ/은 것 같다” (“피곤한”), “이다” “-ㄴ 것 같다”, and the recalled past “-었던 것 같다”. A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-는/-ㄴ”: “살다 → 사는, 산”. It can be about oneself (“배가 고픈 것 같아요”) or others. The polite form is “-는 것 같아요”.

examples.en: It seems to be raining outside.

examples.ko: 민준이는 어제 잠을 못 잔 것 같아요.
examples.en: Minjun seems not to have slept well yesterday.
It looks like it will be cold tomorrow.

examples.ko: 저는 이 색깔이 더 좋은 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think I like this color better.

examples.ko: 열이 나는 것 같아서 병원에 갔다.
examples.en: It seemed that I had a fever, so I went to the hospital.

compare.difference: “-을 것 같다” is a hedge: it looks like. “-을 것이다” states a firmer prediction or intention.

pair.en: It looks like it will rain.
It will rain.

compare.difference: Both guess from evidence. “-는 것 같다” also fits the speaker's own feelings and opinions.

pair.en: Minjun seems to be tired.
Minjun seems to be tired.

pitfalls.note: The past modifier after a vowel is “-ㄴ”: “오다” becomes “온”.
pitfalls.en: It seems to have rained.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-는”.
pitfalls.en: They seem to live in Seoul.

topik_tip: Modifier plus “것 같다”: present “-는”, past “-ㄴ”, future “-ㄹ”; adjectives “-ㄴ”.

label: since, it has been (time elapsed)
meaning_en: An expression for the time that has passed since an event: “it has been N since I X”. It is followed by a time word and “되다, 지나다, 넘다” or “오래되다”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with the past modifier: “오다 → 온 지”, “졸업하다 → 졸업한 지”, “먹다 → 먹은 지”, “만들다 → 만든 지” (the ㄹ drops). “지” is a separate word, written with a space. The frame is “-ㄴ 지 + time + 되다/지나다”; “-ㄴ 지 얼마 안 되다” means “it has not been long since”. It is not used with adjectives. Do not mix it up with the question ending “-는지” (whether).

examples.ko: 한국에 온 지 삼 년이 되었다.
examples.en: It has been three years since I came to Korea.

examples.ko: 대학교를 졸업한 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
examples.en: It has not been long since I graduated from university.
It has been a long time since I was in touch with that friend.

examples.ko: 이 집에 이사 온 지 벌써 십 년이 넘었다.
examples.en: It has already been over ten years since we moved into this house.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹은 지 한 시간밖에 안 지났는데 배가 고파요.
examples.en: Only an hour has passed since I ate, but I am hungry.

compare.difference: “-은 후에” says what comes after in order. “-은 지” counts the time that has gone by since.

pair.en: After coming to Korea, I learned Korean.

pair.ko: 한국에 온 지 삼 년이 되었다.
pair.en: It has been three years since I came to Korea.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ 지” (with a space) counts time; “-는지” (attached) is “whether”.

pair.en: I do not know whether they came.
It has been a long time since they came.

pitfalls.note: The modifier is the past one: “온 지”.
pitfalls.wrong: 한국에 오는 지 삼 년이 되었다.
pitfalls.right: 한국에 온 지 삼 년이 되었다.
pitfalls.en: It has been three years since I came to Korea.

pitfalls.note: “지” is a separate word: write a space.
pitfalls.right: 한국에 온 지 삼 년이 되었다.
pitfalls.en: It has been three years since I came to Korea.

topik_tip: The spacing contrast “온 지” (since) versus “왔는지” (whether) is a known writing-test point.

label: making a noun clause with “것”
meaning_en: An expression that turns a verb or adjective phrase into a noun clause: “doing X, X-ing, that which is X”. It lets a whole action stand as a subject, an object or a complement.
usage: Verbs take “-는 것” (present), “-ㄴ/은 것” (past), “-ㄹ/을 것” (future); adjectives take “-ㄴ/은 것”: “읽다 → 읽는 것”, “예쁘다 → 예쁜 것”, “만들다 → 만드는 것”, “살다 → 사는 것”. The noun clause takes particles (“듣는 것을 좋아하다”, “운동하는 것이 좋다”). It also forms the explaining frame “-는 것이다” (“중요한 것은 ...-는 것이다”). In speech “것” becomes “거” (“먹는 거”). The related “-기” is the shorter form used in fixed frames.

examples.ko: 나는 한국 노래를 듣는 것을 좋아한다.
examples.en: I like listening to Korean songs.
Exercising every day is good for health.
Knowledge is power.
Ask the teacher about what is difficult.
What matters is not giving up.

compare.difference: “-는 것” is the free noun clause. “-기” is shorter and fixed in frames like “-기 쉽다”.

pair.en: I like running.
I like running.

compare.difference: “거” is the spoken contraction of “것”; the meaning is the same.

pair.en: I like eating.
I like eating.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은 것”, not “-는 것”.
pitfalls.en: I bought a pretty one.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-는”.
pitfalls.en: Making food is fun.

topik_tip: The same modifier choice as the adnominal endings: present “-는”, past “-ㄴ”, future “-ㄹ”.

label: while, during
meaning_en: An expression for a stretch of time: “while X is going on, during X”. The main clause happens within or alongside that period. The “에” is optional: “-는 동안”.
usage: Verbs take “-는 동안(에)” (“요리하다 → 요리하는 동안”, “살다 → 사는 동안”); adjectives take “-ㄴ/은 동안”; a noun of time takes “N 동안” (“방학 동안”, “두 시간 동안”). The subjects of the two clauses can be different. It stresses the whole duration, unlike “-을 때”, which points to the time when something happens. “동안” is a separate word.

examples.ko: 내가 요리하는 동안에 동생은 청소를 했다.
examples.en: While I cooked, my younger sibling cleaned.

examples.ko: 한국에 사는 동안 많은 친구를 사귀었다.
examples.en: While living in Korea, I made many friends.

examples.ko: 비가 오는 동안에는 밖에 나갈 수 없었다.
examples.en: While it was raining, we could not go outside.
During the vacation I did a part-time job.

examples.ko: 어머니가 잠깐 자리를 비우는 동안에 아이가 울기 시작했다.
examples.en: While the mother was away for a moment, the child began to cry.

compare.difference: “-으면서” joins two actions of the same subject. “-는 동안” also allows different subjects.

pair.en: I watched television while cooking.
While I cooked, my younger sibling cleaned.

compare.difference: “-을 때” points to a time when something happens; “-는 동안” covers the whole stretch.

pair.en: A call came when I was at home.

pair.ko: 집에 있는 동안 전화가 세 번 왔다.
pair.en: Three calls came while I was at home.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-는”.
pitfalls.wrong: 한국에 살는 동안 친구를 많이 사귀었다.
pitfalls.right: 한국에 사는 동안 친구를 많이 사귀었다.
pitfalls.en: While living in Korea, I made many friends.

pitfalls.note: “동안” is a separate word, written with a space.
pitfalls.en: During the vacation I did a part-time job.

topik_tip: “N 동안” (a period) and “-는 동안” (while doing) are the two shapes; “-는 동안” with a verb is spaced.

label: have done (experience)
meaning_en: An expression for experience: “have done X before, there was a time when I X-ed”. The negative “-ㄴ 적이 없다” says one has never done it.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with the past modifier: “가다 → 간 적이 있다”, “먹다 → 먹은 적이 있다”, “하다 → 한 적이 있다”, “만들다 → 만든 적이 있다” (the ㄹ drops). It is common with “-어 보다”: “가 본 적이 있다” (have been to). It is for experiences at some unspecified time, not for an event at a given time. A past version is “-ㄴ 적이 있었다”. The question “-ㄴ 적이 있어요?” asks whether one has ever done it.

examples.ko: 저는 제주도에 가 본 적이 있어요.
examples.en: I have been to Jeju Island.
Have you ever eaten Korean food?

examples.ko: 그 영화를 본 적이 없어서 내용을 몰라요.
examples.en: I have never seen that movie, so I do not know the story.

examples.ko: 어렸을 때 병원에 입원한 적이 있다.
examples.en: When I was little, I was hospitalized once.

examples.ko: 그 사람과 이야기해 본 적은 없지만 이름은 알아요.
examples.en: I have never talked with that person, but I know the name.

compare.difference: “-었었-” marks a past situation that is over. “-은 적이 있다” says that one has experienced it, at some time.

pair.en: I went to Jeju Island.
I have been to Jeju Island.

compare.difference: “가 봤어요” says one tried or went; “가 본 적이 있어요” stresses having the experience.

pair.en: I have been to Jeju Island.
I have had the experience of going to Jeju Island.

pitfalls.note: The modifier is past: “간 적”.
pitfalls.en: I have been to Seoul.

pitfalls.note: It is for experience at some time, not an event at a stated time.
pitfalls.en: I have been to Seoul.

topik_tip: Experience frames: “-ㄴ 적이 있다/없다”, often with “-어 보다”.

label: do (written order)
meaning_en: A sentence-final form that gives a firm instruction or order in notices, rules and memos: “Do X”. It is impersonal and brief and has no politeness marker.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: after a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ 것”, after other consonants “-을 것”. “끄다 → 끌 것”, “놓다 → 놓을 것”, “제출하다 → 제출할 것”, “만들다 → 만들 것”. The negative instruction is “-지 말 것”. It appears in classroom rules, signs, forms and written notes,. The polite ways to ask are “-세요” or “-어 주세요”. Do not confuse it with “-을 것이다” (future).

examples.en: Turn off mobile phones during class.
Put used items back in place.
Submit the report by tomorrow.
Do not run in the corridor.

examples.ko: 시험 중에는 책을 보지 말고 조용히 할 것.
examples.en: During the exam, do not look at books and keep quiet.

compare.difference: “-으세요” is the polite spoken request. “-을 것” is a terse written order with no politeness.

pair.en: Please submit it by tomorrow.
Submit it by tomorrow.

compare.difference: The same shape with “이다” is a statement about the future; the bare “-을 것” is an order.

pair.en: I will submit it by tomorrow.
Submit it by tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem merges with “-ㄹ”.
pitfalls.en: Make a flag.

topik_tip: The order “-을 것” appears on signs and in rules; the negative is “-지 말 것”.

label: when, at the time of
meaning_en: An expression for the time at which something happens: “when X, at the time of X”. It covers a moment, a period and a habit.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ 때”, after other consonants “-을 때”; it attaches to verbs, adjectives and “이다”: “가다 → 갈 때”, “먹다 → 먹을 때”, “살다 → 살 때”, “어리다 → 어릴 때”, “학생이다 → 학생일 때”. A past stem makes the earlier event complete: “-었을 때”. The tense of “-ㄹ 때” is relative: “갈 때” means on the way or about to go, “갔을 때” means after getting there. “때” is a separate word; “N 때” is also used (“방학 때, 학생 때”).

examples.en: I lived in the countryside when I was little.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹을 때 텔레비전을 보지 마세요.
examples.en: Do not watch television when you eat.
When I went to Korea, I met a friend.
Please call when you have time.

examples.ko: 피곤할 때는 일찍 자는 게 좋다.
examples.en: When you are tired, it is good to sleep early.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 때” is the time during or before the action; “-었을 때” is the time after it has been done.

pair.en: I bought a bag when I was going to Seoul.
I bought a bag when I was in Seoul.

compare.difference: “-을 때” points to a time; “-으면” sets a condition (“once, if”).

pair.en: I will call when I am going home.
I will call once I get home.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem merges with “-ㄹ”.
pitfalls.en: It is fun when I hang out with friends.

pitfalls.note: The future-type modifier is used for a time that has not finished: “먹을 때”.
pitfalls.en: Do not call while I eat.

topik_tip: Pairs like “갈 때 / 갔을 때” (before arriving / after arriving) are a regular exam point.

label: I might (thinking of doing)
meaning_en: An expression for a tentative thought of doing something: “I am thinking I might X, maybe I will X”. It is the speaker's half-formed intention, said to themselves or to a listener.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: after a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ까 보다”, after other consonants “-을까 보다”; the polite form is “-ㄹ까 봐요”. The subject is the speaker, and the idea is often a casual or spur-of-the-moment plan (“영화나 볼까 봐요”). Do not mix it up with “-ㄹ까 봐” (afraid that) which is a worry: “비가 올까 봐 우산을 가져왔다”. The stem is a verb of intended action.

examples.en: I am thinking I might go home early today.
The weather is nice, so I might take a walk or something.
I am so tired that I am thinking of quitting my job.
I am thinking I might move next month.

examples.ko: 주말에 영화나 한 편 볼까 보다.
examples.en: I might watch a movie or so this weekend.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ까 하다” (“갈까 해요”) is a near-synonym: a tentative plan. “-ㄹ까 보다” sounds more like thinking aloud.

pair.en: I am thinking of going early today.
I might go early today.

compare.difference: “-으려고 하다” is a plan that is firmer; “-ㄹ까 보다” is still open.

pair.en: I intend to move.
I might move.

pitfalls.note: The worry pattern is “-ㄹ까 봐” (afraid that); do not use “보다”.
pitfalls.en: I brought an umbrella in case it rained.

pitfalls.note: The subject is the speaker: it is not a plan of a third person.
pitfalls.en: I am thinking I might go early.

topik_tip: “-ㄹ까 보다” (maybe I will) and “-ㄹ까 봐” (worried that) differ in the last syllable and in meaning.

label: try doing
meaning_en: An expression for trying something out or having a go: “try X-ing, give X a try”. With “-ㄴ 적이 있다” it is experience; as “-어 보세요” it is a friendly suggestion.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with “-아/어”: “먹다 → 먹어 보다”, “입다 → 입어 보다”, “가다 → 가 보다”, “듣다 → 들어 보다” (ㄷ-irregular), “돕다 → 도와 보다”. In speech the polite shape is “-어 보세요, -어 봤어요”. “한번” strengthens the tentative feel (“한번 해 보세요”). It does not mean “see” here: the helper “보다” only marks a trial. Another pattern, “-어 보이다”, means “looks”.

examples.en: Please try this on.

examples.ko: 김치를 먹어 봤는데 생각보다 맵지 않았어요.
examples.en: I tried kimchi, and it was not as spicy as I thought.
If you do not know, try asking the teacher.
Let's try meeting up this weekend.
I tried looking for the book in the library, but it was not there.

compare.difference: “-어 보다” is to try; “-어 보이다” is to look. The two sentences differ by one sound.

pair.en: Try this food.
This food looks tasty.

compare.difference: “-어 봤다” says that one tried; “-어 본 적이 있다” says that one has had the experience.

pair.en: I tried kimchi.
I have eaten kimchi before.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular verb turns ㄷ into ㄹ before “-어”.
pitfalls.en: Please try listening to this song.

pitfalls.note: “-고 보다” has a different meaning (find out after doing).
pitfalls.en: Please try this on.

topik_tip: The helper “보다” here only means “try”; “-어 보세요” is the standard invitation.
